utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Good morning. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning, to the technical booth. The interpreters are here, are they? Good morning. Good morning to the legal assistants, the court reporters. Good morning to the Prosecution; good morning to the Defence; I see that they are all here. Good morning to the accused. So we are going to resume our case, Kvocka and others. We're saying this for the benefit of the record. It is up to the Prosecutor this morning, Madam Hollis or Mr. Michael Keegan, who are going to tell us what we are going to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, to give you an update of where we are in terms of the late disclosure, as of today, we are current with disclosure on Witness AI; on this witness, Mr. Oklopcic; on Witness B, who is number 6 on the list. Witness number 7 has been moved to another slot because of her personal circumstances. Witness number 8, we are current. Witness number 9, we are current. Witness number 10 has been moved to another spot because of witness 10's personal circumstances. Witness number 11, we are current except for one B/C/S version of a transcript that is to be delivered to us today, which will be served on the Defence today. Witness number 12 is current. Witness number 13 is current except for a short affidavit, which will be filed with the Defence today. Witness number 14 is current except for a B/C/S translation of a statement, which should be filed today. Witness number 3, Witness AK, is current except for a videotape that we're attempting to find which may contain an interview of this witness. We don't have that video yet. So we're prepared to proceed with Mr. Oklopcic, and thereafter with witness 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Madam Hollis. Please sit down for the moment. Before resuming the normal course of work, the Chamber would like to convey to the parties its extreme concern regarding the situation with the witnesses in our case. For reasons which you are all well aware of, and which are in the public domain, several witnesses have had to spend several days in The Hague; others have left and have to come back, and for one of them, he will be coming for the third time. We must do everything we can to avoid having witnesses confronted with such difficulties. The Chamber says this in relation to the witnesses of the Prosecution, and this also applies to the witnesses of the Defence. It is not only a budgetary problem, although the costs are considerable, but it is, above all, a question of principle. We cannot function without the indispensable assistance provided to us by the witnesses. But for the majority of them, they are not only witnesses; they are, in the first place, victims who are coming to convey here their suffering, the suffering of their loved ones and their friends. This applies both to the witnesses called by the Prosecution and by the Defence. We must all do everything we can to convey to them the feeling of interest that we have in them so that they may testify under the most serene conditions. It is in the interest of the credibility of our system of justice. I also wish to express my most sincerest thanks in my own name, but I think I can also speak on behalf of all of us, to the commander of the Victims and Witnesses Unit who has accomplished an admirable task. I will once again be most grateful to you for doing everything so as to facilitate the testimony of the witnesses and to make their appearance as short and as necessary as possible. If we are all vigilant, we will ensure a better justice and a more humane justice to be handed down. To achieve that, the Chamber orders the parties to submit to the Chamber a list of witnesses which they are going to call to testify in the week, that is, seven working days in advance. We must have a list of witnesses who are going to testify during the week. I think that this can assist the parties to organise themselves, to be more disciplined, so as to avoid bringing witnesses who are not going to testify and who only have to wait. I think you understand well the aims behind this decision. I see that Mr. O'Sullivan had the intention to speak. Mr. O'Sullivan, do you have anything to communicate to us?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you, and good morning. The Defence wishes to raise another matter with the Trial Chamber before the witness Oklopcic enters the courtroom. On Tuesday, May 9th, Your Honours, we adjourned, with the witness Oklopcic having completed his examination-in-chief; the cross-examination by the Defence has not yet begun. Your Honours will recall that on May 3rd you issued an order in relation to witnesses who are under oath. Your Honours ordered that "without leave of the Trial Chamber, all contacts shall be prohibited between the parties and a witness after the witness has taken the solemn declaration, until he or she has completed his or her testimony." Last Tuesday, May 9th, during the break in proceedings between 11.00 and 11.30, witness Oklopcic was observed in the witness room, which is located just outside the courtroom, in conversation with Mr. Keegan of the Prosecution, who at that time was leading Mr. Oklopcic in examination-in-chief. It appears, Your Honours, that your order has been breached by the Prosecution. I must be perfectly clear of the reason why the Defence is raising this issue. We are not raising this matter to suggest that Mr. Keegan's integrity has been or should be brought into question. Our position is this: There appears to have been a prima facie breach of your order. Can I remind Your Honours that in issuing the order, you emphasised that contact must cease because when a witness appears before the Trial Chamber he or she is less a witness of a party but more a witness of justice. In our submission, one way of explaining the rationale of your order is to say that justice must not only be done, it must be seen to be done. This is central to the credibility of a justice system. If, as it appears, your order has been breached by the Prosecution, in the interests of justice, we submit that the appropriate remedy is this: The evidence in chief given by the witness Oklopcic following the break in proceedings between 11.00 a.m. and 11.30 a.m., last Tuesday, May 9th, that evidence should be struck from the record, or alternatively Your Honours should completely disregard that evidence. Those are my submissions in relation to this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. O'Sullivan. You may be seated. I will give the Prosecution a chance to respond and explain. Mr. Keegan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honours. Just so all the facts are on the record, during the break, of course I went to the witness room for the purpose of letting the other witnesses who were to follow Mr. Oklopcic know what the situation was. The difficulty is, of course, there's only one witness room available. Apparently the other witness waiting room that was near this one has been taken away from the Victims and Witnesses Unit. Mrs. Nikolic actually saw me because the Defence counsel use the same door to get out to the patio, and she raised the issue with me and, in fact, I showed her that unfortunately the other witnesses were also in that room as well, which of course presents an obvious difficulty which I indicated to her. And I made it clear that I was speaking to the other witnesses and I couldn't help the fact that Mr. Oklopcic was also in that room. He, in fact, attempted to say something to me, like, "When are we going to start again," and I simply told him through the translator, "I'm not allowed to have contact with you at this point." We're very aware of the difficulty in the perception issue. At the same time, there was no Victims and Witnesses Unit personnel present, and there has not been any Victims and Witnesses Unit personnel present with our witnesses since this trial began. They say they don't have enough people. They indicate that they periodically send someone to check on the witnesses who are waiting, but there's no one in there so there's not even an intermediary to whom I could address the issue. I, unfortunately, was in the position of having to speak to the other witnesses directly. Fortunately one of our language assistants was present with the witnesses who were waiting, but not yet been called, and so I was able to facilitate that message. We raised the issue with the Victims and Witnesses Unit that day about our concern because of this very real problem, and we understand the perception it can present. They indicated they are trying to do something, but they don't yet have a solution as to how they can separate witnesses who've already taken an oath and those who have not. So that was the nature of the contact, and I can assure the Court there was no discussion between myself and Mr. Oklopcic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: As I said, this was not raised to question Mr. Keegan's integrity. However, and I'm not sure how far we want to pursue this, the contact we were referring to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. Having heard this explanation given by Mr. Keegan, what is your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The contact I was referring to occurred between 11.00 and 11.30, and my understanding is the contact Mr. Keegan had with Mrs. Nikolic was after the proceedings, after we broke. I was referring to a different period when Mr. Keegan was observed with Mr. Oklopcic, that is, between 11.00 and 11.30. My understanding is Mrs. Nikolic saw him after that, after we had completed proceedings for the day. And that is the basis for our request to have the testimony struck or disregarded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your opinion, is it necessary to conduct an inquiry to clarify all these circumstances, or do you still maintain your request?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I don't know if Mr. Keegan recalls the event I'm speaking of, the one that occurred between 11.00 and 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw that Mr. Keegan was on his feet. Mr. Keegan, have we finished with this matter? You know that the witnesses are waiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. As far as I know, if there was -- the only one I recall is the one when I had a conversation with Mrs. Nikolic. If there was another instance, it would have been in the same light; that is, I was addressing the other witnesses who happened to be in the room, and unfortunately, again, the witness who has already taken the oath is put in the same place. But I can affirm to the Court that I had absolutely no contact with the witness other than to tell the witness we're not allowed to speak any more because I am not sure they got that instruction directly from the Victims and Witnesses Unit, and maybe that needs to be reaffirmed as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Keegan, if I understand well, you went to this room because you wanted to talk to witnesses who were testifying, and Oklopcic was among those witnesses. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No. I was speaking to tell the witnesses who had not yet been called, Your Honour, because they are waiting in the room. As I said, because there is no one with them, they never understand what is going on. They want to know how much longer they will be in the room, when they might get to the stand, those kinds of things. So on every break we try and reassure the witnesses where we are in procedure, whether they are going to be called, those kinds of things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber has heard the parties on this matter. We are not certain, at least, that Mr. Keegan did this intentionally. We agree that it happened by chance, and even if it did not, the Chamber is certainly going to take measures with the Witnesses Unit so that we can have a situation which will facilitate contact of the parties with the witnesses who've still not taken a solemn declaration and to avoid the witnesses being together, because otherwise there will still be doubts. So we have a logistical situation which has contributed to this possibility. Therefore, to be, or to appear to be, these are things that may be confused and we must therefore regulate this situation so that at the same time, appearances will correspond to facts. And we will talk to the Victims and Witnesses Unit to avoid this situation of having the witnesses together, those who've not taken a solemn declaration which the parties may contact, and those who've already taken the solemn declaration and with whom no further contacts with allowed. Therefore, we are fully aware of this situation, and as O'Sullivan have reminded us, we wish to confirm that these witnesses are witnesses of justice and that is why we have issued this other order. The Chamber is concerned about the witnesses, both those called by the Defence and those by the Prosecution, and this situation has to be cleared up so as to avoid tomorrow Mr. Keegan saying, "I saw one of you contacting a witness who has not taken the solemn declaration but who happened to be with another witness who already has," and we must clear up this situation fully. For the moment, what we are going to do is that we are going to declare this incident closed. So we are going to resume with the cross-examination of Mr. Oklopcic, and I should like to know, Mr. Krstan Simic, what is the order in which you will cross-examine? I think you have already told us, but could you remind us, please? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the order will be slightly changed today. The first will be representatives of Mr. Kos' Defence team, then myself, then representatives of Mr. Radic's Defence team, then Mr. Prcac's, and at the end Mr. Zigic's Defence attorney. So there is a minor change in the order in relation to the standard order of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Simic. Can we have the witness brought in, please? Yes, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While the witness is coming in, I would just like to take advantage of the time. Let the witness come in. I would just like to take advantage of a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have not received the order of witnesses for this week from the Prosecution, so we don't know who is going to testify, and secondly, there seems to be a difference between Mrs. Hollis and us regarding the numbers, the order of the witnesses, the numbers attributed to witnesses, because when she read out the list, the names and the numbers do not correspond. For example, Mr. Oklopcic is, in our list, number 5. Is he the same number in Ms. Hollis' list? As for the others that she mentioned today, they are not given the same numbers that she mentioned, and this may cause some confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the list from which I was reading is the confidential annex to the updated list of witnesses filed on the 28th of April, and the numbers are the same that I read out as are on that list which was served on the Defence. Those were the numbers I was using to avoid any confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Ms. Hollis. The 25th of April or the 28th of April?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: 28th, Your Honour. 28th of April, updated, Prosecution more list of changes to witnesses, the confidential annex, updated list of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because in the translation, I got the 25th, but I see the 28th in the transcript. It is the list that I have in my hands, is it not? Does it correspond? Does that meet the difficulties of Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Let me give you an example. AI is numbered 4 on this list, and she read it out as number 2 today, (redacted) (redacted).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Number 2 is Witness AJ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] AJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's all right, then. It's all right. But this morning, you said he was under number 4, not number 2. And who is going to testify today? Can we have the number, please? After Mr. Oklopcic, who will be the next witness, so we know, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Witness AK, witness number 3, followed by witness number 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that clear now? We have to try to communicate well. Perhaps we always need to mention the document, as you have done now. There are 12 attorneys so there may be some confusion. So this is the list, filed on the 28th of April this year. So when Ms. Hollis mentions numbers 1 and 2, it is from that list. So, Ms. Hollis, that is why it is good to have at least seven days in advance the list of witnesses that we're going to call that week. In that way, there will be no problems, I think. That can facilitate the proceedings and avoid witnesses waiting for 15 days. I'm sorry for saying this, but we must organise ourselves, that is our duty. If we need five witnesses for a week, we will call five witnesses for that week, not 10, not 15. The Chamber prefers to have time that is not filled or used on Friday than having a witness who will start with one hour and have to stay over until Monday. Can you pay attention to that, please? Respect persons. Witnesses are persons, and that is what we must do. And if we organise ourselves better, I'm sure we will improve things for ourselves and for the witnesses. And if we have a protected witness, and I say "protected," and he waits here for 15 days, what justification can we have for that? I'm addressing myself to both the Prosecution and the Defence. It is the same for both parties. I apologise, Ms. Hollis. Please convey to us any difficulties that you may have. Perhaps we can help by talking about them. Please sit down, Madam Hollis. Thank you very much. I now give the floor to the Nikolic Defence team, Mr. Nikolic, for the cross-examination of Mr. Oklopcic. Good morning, Mr. Oklopcic. Can you hear me? It's the President talking to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for the inconvenience caused to you, but in any event we are beginning with your cross-examination. I must remind you that you are still under oath. You have told us that you will tell us the whole truth, nothing but the truth. And now you are going to answer questions which Mr. Nikolic is going to put to you on behalf of the Defence. Thank you. You have the floor, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please Mr. Nikolic, microphone, please. And will you speak into the microphone, please. Cross-examined by Mr. Nikolic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have several questions for you, to which I hope you will provide simple answers. You had a meeting with investigators of the Prosecution and you gave a statement in 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to ask the usher to give Mr. Oklopcic the original English version and the B/C/S version. Could the usher please provide Your Honours with three English versions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Oklopcic, you have two texts in front of you; one is in English, the other is in the B/C/S language. The B/C/S language was given to you so that you can follow my questions more easily. Mr. Oklopcic, will you please look at the cover page of the B/C/S version. It says on top, "The International Criminal Tribunal for the prosecution of persons responsible for serious violations of international law committed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia since 1991." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Below that it says, "Witness statement"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On this cover page, we can see the date of the interview. Are the dates correct?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please look at the English version of that text. There is your signature at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please look through the English version and see whether each page has been signed by you?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it has.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should like to ask you to look at the B/C/S version, on the last page of that version, where it says the date, "the 10th of December, 1994," and signature of the witness. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look at the last page of the English version. You signed that statement, dated the 10th of December, 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, but it is my signature, yes. Whether that is the date, it probably is. It is my signature, that is for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Oklopcic, is it true that you gave this statement of your own free will, without any pressure?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you made that statement, you told the truth.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to tell the truth, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You made that statement over a period of six days, on the 22nd, the 23rd, the 24th, the 25th, and the 26th of September, 1994, and on the 10th of December, 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember roughly, on average, how much time did you spend talking to the investigators?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About eight hours every day, a working day on an average.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Every day, eight hours on an average.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Three persons were present when this interview was taken. If you look at the cover page, you will see the names?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. They put questions to you, and you provided the answers.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you tell them something of your own accord?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that question now. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you said "probably."

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you made that statement, there was no pressure brought to bear on you.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke of your own free will.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of my own free will.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your interview occurred roughly two days after the relevant events in the Omarska camp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Two years, I'm sorry. Two years, not two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The events were still fresh in your mind; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your statement is about 29 pages long, and it is full of details; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you made that statement, you gave the best rendering you could of what you could remember.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of what I could remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Oklopcic, did you know that this statement would be used in trial proceedings in the International Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assumed it would.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, you did?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you turn to page 23. In your statement, on page 23, on page 23, the one but last paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the English version, it is page 31, third paragraph from the top.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- you mentioned the nickname Krle; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you agree with me, in view of this statement, that in that statement you never mentioned a person with the nickname Krle ever again in relation to any incident?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I can, if you say so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no further questions. I would like to ask Your Honours to admit this statement into evidence. It is D2/2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Keegan, do you have any objections to the admission of this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: We have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dubuisson.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As mentioned, it is D2/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. Thank you very much, Mr. Nikolic. We are now going to go on to Mr. Krstan Simic. Cross-examined by Mr. K. Simic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Oklopcic, Mr. Nikolic asked you a few questions which I myself had the intention of asking you. So in order not to repeat those questions, your statements which you gave are quite clear, and your statements were made of your own free will and signed as such. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Talking about the statement, I should like to ask you to try and recall on how many occasions and with what persons did you talk about the events relating to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking about the investigators or all persons in general?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The total number of persons that you talked to.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sincerely speaking, there were quite a few visits by the investigators who came to seek me out and talk to me. As regards other people that I talked about with the events in Omarska, that was quite infrequent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I'm talking about official institutions and representatives of those institutions.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for those, I only had four or five encounters with the investigators of the court who came to see me at my home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this mean that the statements of the 22nd, 23rd, 24th, 25th, and 26th September of 1994, then we have another statement of the 10th of December, 1994?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. So we have two occasions, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you talk to the representatives of the Tribunal in June 1995?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall the exact date, but I did talk to them after these occasions. I cannot recall the exact dates and the exact months. It is quite impossible, you know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know whether to ask you this. I have a statement here from the 22nd of June, but we'll revert to that particular statement a bit later. Talking about these statements, as Mr. Nikolic gave you the text of the statement which you have before you, you polemicise in several places in that statement with another statement that you yourself had given without particularly stating to whom and on which particular occasion. It just refers to some discrepancies. What is this about?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what you're talking about. Can you give me a specific example?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 9, last paragraph. Let me just find the English version. Page 12 of the English version, the last paragraph. I understand there that the report of my interview that it's deleted, states among other things, and then it goes on to state the rest of it. Do you recall that statement?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know what is deleted here. I really cannot respond to this question, although I do want to give you an answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not interested in what is deleted, I want to know whether you recall to whom you talked when you gave this particular statement. What statement are you referring to? To whom did you give it and when?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is stated here, right in the beginning. Mr. Tieger --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, you don't understand me. Mr. Oklopcic, you talked to the gentlemen who were interrogating you, and you were explaining to them. I know that in a record of some other statement, of some other interview with me there was something said which differs from what I am saying now. What particular record are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm able to read, this is not what this says. I understand that the report of my interview states, "among other things," that is what I said, inter alia, not that there had been any changes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, Mr. Oklopcic, this is not the subject. What particular minutes, what particular record/statement, are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I really cannot remember at this point. I cannot recall that particular statement/record.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the occasion of the June 1995 visit, did the interrogators give you any photographs to identify?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did, once. Whether that took place in 1995, on that particular occasion, I don't know. But I did identify some persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many photographs were there?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think six. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise anyone on those photographs?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I cannot recall now. I cannot give you an answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that verified in the record?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It ought to have been -- I was not the one conducting the interview or taking notes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you sign the photographs that you identified?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have an objection to raise. We have not been disclosed these photographs, we have not seen these photographs up to now, so that we have no way of ascertaining which particular photographs were shown to Mr. Oklopcic. We feel that we should, after all, be shown these photographs in order for the Defence to be able to prepare its witness interrogation in the proper and efficient way, particularly in connection with Mr. Oklopcic's statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Oklopcic, on the 20th of May, you testified that you were a participant in a football match of veterans.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was on the 20th or the 30th. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that during that match you heard a burst of fire from the direction of Hambarine; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And you could also see smoke.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later on you said that at the time you had no information but that you learned from the media what had happened; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And not only from the media, but the night among -- from other people, from stories told by others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your testimony, you covered this event rather quickly, even though it was a dramatic and tragic event.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you hear from the media, or in contact with other persons? What had happened around the 20th of May?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a shooting incident at a checkpoint in front of Hambarine -- I don't know if you know the area; there is a slope there -- and in front of Hambarine there was a checkpoint, as throughout town Serbian guards and military had checkpoints. And so the citizens of Hambarine decided to set up their own checkpoint, and that is where the shooting incident had occurred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the consequences of the shooting?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The consequences were that an ultimatum was issued -- what do you mean the consequences?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean regarding the casualties?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the consequences were. I think two were killed and two were wounded among the Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Slowly, please, Mr. Oklopcic. Will you please answer my questions?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am answering your questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am asking you whether it is correct that in that incident, at the Hambarine checkpoint, two men were killed and another two were wounded of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what Serb television announced. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Yes, we'll try to slow down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have just mentioned checkpoints. What were they, really?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Checkpoints consisted of 10 or 15 sacks of sand and two to three or three or four soldiers under arms manning them, or policemen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Oklopcic, who did these checkpoints belong to throughout the territory of Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the town itself, because in fact I lived in the centre of town, the checkpoint was held by the Serb side, the soldiers and police. In the Muslim villages around it, Kozarac or Hambarine, for example, because I worked in Kozarac for a time, and Trnopolje, but in Kozarac, on the one hand there was the Territorial Defence of Kozarac, the checkpoint, and opposite, on the crossroads of Banja Luka, Prijedor, and Kozarac, there was the checkpoint of the Yugoslav army and police. And at Hambarine as well, there was this checkpoint underneath Hambarine, at the very approach to Hambarine, there was a Territorial Defence checkpoint which organised that particular checkpoint and set it up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we take it, then, that at the end of May, in the Prijedor municipality, in fact there was a division, a division had been made of the ethnic communities at checkpoints, and they were armed and prevented the free passage of people and traffic and so on.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we cannot say that because taking over power on the 30th of April by the Serb side, at that particular point, all the checkpoints were held by the Serb side. The checkpoint in Hambarine was a response to the Serbian side and provocation from them, because drunken guards, soldiers, and policemen would march, that is to say, they would drive by with the three-finger sign and fire, and I'm very sorry to say that those Serb soldiers died. But this was the result of provocation on the part of the drunken passers-by. And I happened to see that on my way to Kozarac and Trnopolje. So the checkpoints at Kozarac and Hambarine, as far as I know, and I repeat, as far as I know, were set up as the result of the taking over of authority by the Serbian army and police on the 30th of April, 1992. And not a day -- one day after, but perhaps 15 or 20 days later, if I may just finish that answer to your question -- if you don't want me to, I'll stop there --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please do go on.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, we had a meeting, that is, the citizens of Raskovac, we had a meeting with Mr. Kusorac [phoen] in May 1992 and we asked why it was only the Serb side and the Serb soldiers that manned these checkpoints, and that was that famous meeting at the Polijne stadium. He laughed, he tried to explain something, but that was it. And as a result of that, we have the intervention well, it wasn't the intervention, but it was the establishment of a checkpoint in Hambarine and Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The checkpoint at the entrance to Hambarine, or to Prijedor, where the Serb checkpoint was, did it prevent people -- prevent the free passage of people without being stopped, having to show their IDs, being searched and so on?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally was stopped at the checkpoint towards the school. The soldiers came and asked for our ID cards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that means that those checkpoints did restrict the freedom of movement, freedom of passage.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I experienced them, yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the ethnic composition of the checkpoint at Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably Muslim because the whole population was Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you happen to hear who took part in this tragic shooting?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. You mean -- yes, there was Aziz Aliskovic, the policeman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they able, in the usual way, to conduct all the necessary things in a criminal investigation? Was a criminal investigation enabled?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot be certain, but I know that one day later, an ultimatum was posed to the population of Hambarine to give up Aziz Aliskovic to the authorities, to give him up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Aliskovic taken into custody ever with respect to this incident?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I didn't see that he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have now rounded off that topic relating to the events that you passed over very quickly. But let us now go back a bit to another topic, the topic of your military involvement. You state in your statement that you did your military service, compulsory military service, in the infantry and that as a sportsman and as an intellectual you advanced very quickly, and received the highest rank in the non-commissioned officers, Sergeant First Class?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as sergeant first class, you were the commander of what?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the commander of a platoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many members does a platoon have?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I recall, if each platoon has four groups, then that would make it eight to ten soldiers, wouldn't it? Eight times four is 32, so let us say 30 to 35 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you, as a reserve officer, had 30 soldiers under you during the exercises. So you were in the reserve formation?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the unit was Karlica, Karlica, Zoran or Zorka, I don't quite remember, but Karlica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he an active officer or reserve officer?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was first of all a reserve, and then he wasn't. He got the rank of lieutenant and captain first class.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the overall unit?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Major Grbic, I believe, as far as I recall. And then there were a few more lieutenants, Lieutenant-Colonel Fokumce [phoen], warrant officer first class, second class. But as I say, that was a long time ago. But Major Grbic and Lieutenant-Colonel Poplvica [phoen].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As somebody who was in town and near all those organs, when you completed the army, what were your duties as a soldier?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To respond to a call-up and to take part in the defence of the former joint state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now when you left the army, did you go to the ministry to sign up, to register?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, it was the Territorial Defence. I don't know which department, but we had to register and become reservists. We had to register once or twice a year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you became a member of the reserve formation of the Yugoslav People's Army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any other members of the reserve formation of recruits, the reserve police force?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a reserve police force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That means that there was this military duty as well, as a member of the reserve police force. Let us round off that topic. Did you have a any work duties to perform?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a work duty but I didn't have any obligation in that respect, to perform a work duty. It is difficult for me to give you an answer when you say "work duty". What do you mean by "work duty"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, for example, if you're called up to have a particular duty to perform?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, I didn't really, because I was a professor, I was a teacher, so there wasn't much there that I could do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As we have covered this system of reserve formations and mobilisation in general, I should like to attempt to ascertain things about the Omarska camp. Did you happen to notice any members in the guards from the reserve formation of the police, or as it was called at the time, the militia?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and there was a difference.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, then. Within the composition, there were members of the reserve police force there.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and the regular police force as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, the regular police force, I understand that. But throughout the compound in Omarska, were there any members of the reserve formation of the army who provided security for the camp?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the time they were all soldiers, they all wore uniforms. I see no reason -- I see no difference between those who were active and those who were reservists, because every Serb had a uniform, had a rifle, and goodness knows what else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So you too as a reservist had a uniform and rifle, did you not?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have a rifle at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the reservist formations. What was the difference between you, for example, and an active, let us say, an active corporal?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was a difference just in rank, but the uniform was the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the officer's uniforms?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't have an officer's uniform. I had an ordinary uniform with my rank on the shoulder.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what I'm asking you. You were a reservist, you were a lance corporal -- a corporal, I'm sorry, and that was a professional calling. And as an ordinary observer, was I able to note the difference if I looked at your uniforms?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you would be able to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you see the difference in the uniforms of the regular formations and the police or active policeman and professional policeman, and the reservists, the reserve police force?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you could and you couldn't. I'm going to answer that question, if I may.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When we're talking about soldiers, could you tell the difference between active-duty policemen and the reserve force in the army and the others? The reserve police force and the active-duty police force?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that was the answer that I wanted to get. In Omarska, in the security system that prevailed in Omarska, you had these three structures; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all three were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That means, let us clarify this once again, within the security system, there was the reserve police force, there were active-duty policemen, and the reserve army formation, as well as active-duty soldiers.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us round off the topic of security. You mentioned that at the beginning of June, within the frameworks of the Omarska compound, there was the special police unit, a special formation. They were the special purpose unit from Banja Luka. Did they have different uniforms, were you able to differentiate them?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't but they had more weapons on them than the other ones, the locals who would come from Omarska or all around Omarska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know that a lot of time has gone by since that time, but could you try and tell us how long they would stay in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One or two weeks. One or two weeks, I know that for sure, and I can give you a very precise answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During their stay, while they were there, were there any shifts of any kind? Did one group of people replace another?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean whether somebody replaced them?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In these special units, elite units.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They came and they were in charge during that first week or two. Then they disappeared and then the other people came, who took over, if we can use that term "took over" command of the camp, or whatever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have just said, in the first days, the people at the head of this unit were in charge. That's what you said a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us who those people were?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't because they were from Banja Luka and they said that they were from Banja Luka themselves, and I didn't know any of these people. I couldn't give you a single name. I don't know that. I would happily give you a name if I knew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know who was the commander of that unit.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a relatively young man, about 30 years old. He was in command of that unit, that's what I know, and mostly there were young people, members of the unit were young people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this younger man, when did he leave Omarska?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they all left Omarska, one or two weeks later. Suddenly they would get their things together and leave. APCs would come by and they left. It wasn't a big unit, it was, say, 15 to 20 men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see the kind of tasks and duties they had to perform, what their role was in the security system?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they stood on the pista in front of the toilets, in front of the entrance to the main building, in front of the hangar and so on. What they wanted, I don't know. I can't enter in their minds to know what they had in mind. THE COURT REPORTER: Would counsel please slow down? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any classical guards?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by classical guards? For me, all guards were guards. They had rifles, they had pistols. I can't see the difference between one guard and another, if you understand me. So I have to answer your question in that way. What do you mean classical guards? They were all classical guards, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who organised their food for them?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the food came from Omarska, their meals came from Omarska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When we are talking about the composition of the security system, do you mean the special forces from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, just a minute, I'll explain what I mean. This active duty and reserve formation, composed of the two, from the Omarska police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember or calculate how many active-duty policemen there were?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of those who were there throughout, who were frequently there, that is to say, Kvocka, Radic, and the others, but every day, every day when five or six new prisoners were brought in, then policemen would come from Prijedor. There was not a single policeman from Prijedor or Omarska who was not at one time in the Omarska camp, who did not come to the camp. So believe me when I say that. And most of them were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Oklopcic, let us try to be as clear as possible. I asked you a clear-cut question related to the security composition from the police station in Omarska and not people who would bring in detainees or come in for any other business. So could you try and answer the question in that way?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me how many policemen there were, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the security of the camp?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I told you, there was Kvocka, there was Radic, they were the ones I saw and the ones I remember, and the others, well, I won't mention the others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the rest, were they reservists?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were reservists and active-duty regular ones. It was never only the reservist formation. It was a mixed group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking who went in, who came, but who stood guard. Who stood guard?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody stood guard of the regular policemen, let me tell you that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us now go back to the security system once again. In your statement you mention a certain person called Stupar.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked that that name not be mentioned. I do not wish him to be mentioned. You can refer to him as ZM or whatever, but I don't want his name to be mentioned. That was a bit of a provocation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, that was no kind of provocation, and these matters are talked about far more freely. I don't mean out of fear. You needn't fear for Mr. Stupar because we look upon him with sympathy.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not afraid of him, and were I afraid I would not have --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to interfere in the debate, but it is absolutely too fast for the interpreters, and certainly for the court reporters. They are not able to follow the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have also noticed this. Please don't speak at the same time. If the witness and Mr. Simic speak at the same time, it is impossible to translate. It is anyway difficult. But if you speak at the same time, it is absolutely impossible. I would like to ask Mr. Simic to put questions in accordance with the Rules, in a clear, specific, and concise manner. In that way, we will proceed more quickly. Perhaps you could finish by 11.00. It would be good. I'm not pressuring you, but go to concrete matters, put specific questions to the witness and you will get concrete answers, Mr. Simic. Continue, please, and do not forget that there are the interpreters as your intermediaries between the two of you. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Oklopcic, do you know Mr. Stupar?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is Mr. Stupar?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My colleague. He worked as a teacher in the primary school called Brane Copija in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was he during the events at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stupar, you mean? He would come into the Omarska concentration camp frequently. He didn't stand guard or anything like that. He would come by from time to time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was a member of the police or the army?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a member of the army. He had a green uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The unit to which he belonged, did it provide security for the Omarska compound?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't answer that question. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you talk to Mr. Stupar?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I talked to him on many occasions in the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a friend, did he try and help you?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did, and he did help me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did he help you?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would bring me food sometimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he talk to any of the official people there, the people in authority there, with respect to your status and to solving it?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did he talk to?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To Rosic, and his father and him were the proprietors of a cafe, a restaurant in Omarska, which was called the Munich Cafe. Probably his father worked abroad, perhaps in Munich, so that's the name he gave to his cafe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he talk to any of the official people from the power structure?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rosic was an official person from the power structure. It was that particular young man Rosic, that was him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he talk to Mr. Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did, he talked to Mr. Drljaca as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the result of those talks?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He tried to get me a permit to be released from the Omarska concentration camp, at least that's what he told me and I believe him; that is to say, I believed him at the time, I really did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That means that this was with respect to your release. He talked to Mr. Rosic and Mr. Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To anybody else?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the guards and some other people. But these are the two names that I know of specifically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Oklopcic, when you testified, you said, and I have the minutes here, that Mr. Meakic was the commander, that is to say, the head of security, and that you assumed that his deputy was Mr. Kvocka. And then you go on to enumerate four reasons which lead you to make that assumption. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know the organisational structure of the police of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Not to use the actual official title.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know the organisation of the police in Prijedor, that is to say, the Public Security Station, as it was referred to?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know the organisation but I knew most of the people there. Who was the chief of the SUP, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I want to ask you something in a slightly different direction. Did you know the rules and regulations, that is to say, in which way appointments were made and distribution of officers to different posts?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you -- were you acquainted with the rules regulating the way in which rifles were borne, that is to say, what officer was entitled to which type of weapon? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] The witness gave an answer, and he said no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So could you repeat for the LiveNote, please.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you happen to know the organisation and way in which disciplinary procedure was conducted?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you spoke about the reasons on which you base your assumption, as you said, you mentioned a person called respect [Realtime transcript read in error "Despot"].

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is a comment to the LiveNote again. We're talking about the -- we were talking about respect, the term "respect," and the transcript has it as Despot.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I mentioned the respect of the guards to their superiors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, well I'll go on to ask you what respect is. In every society, there are people who are professionals, who are honourable, who have high moral qualities.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They do, yes. They do exist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You admit that they do exist. Now, in everyday life, we always show respect towards people of that kind, do we not?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said -- you made your assumption and you say that this was confirmed by the fact that Mr. Kvocka brought food to the guards.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not food during lunchtime, but they were in-between meals, snacks, and during the night. Food, drinks, and cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Oklopcic, you were an officer. Now, in what system does the superior serve his subordinates and plays this role of somebody who runs their errands?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what system this is done. I just told you what I saw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wanted to take note of the fact that you don't know which system this can happen in.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I stand by what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should now like to ask you some questions about the flag. Where was the flag pole, and you mentioned the raising of a flag. Where was that?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we came to Omarska, at the beginning, two or three weeks after that, it did not exist, that flag pole didn't exist. After a certain amount of time, it sort of appear, and it was a pole that was placed in front of the tap and the canteen, or the main central building there [indicates], loud and clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you show us, please, where this was?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. It was at this position here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there was a concrete slab underneath; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, how was this crooked pole put in there?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, but I know that a flag was placed there. Not at first but later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was a crooked pole on this concrete slab. When was this?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning, when the shifts replaced each other, they would line up and hand over the shift, and we were usually on the pista, because I spent most of my time on the pista, and then we too had to get up and stand to attention during the raising of the flag ceremony. And this was not done always but there was one shift in particular which liked to raise the flag. This was not done every day. Sometimes they would forget. I don't know. We didn't mind one way or another whether they would raise the flag or not. That was the least of our problems. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it is now 11.00, and I have some 15 minutes of some very important questions. May we have the break? We have just established contact it appears, and Mr. Oklopcic has started answering my questions with clearer answers. So I respect the objections, but I would like to say that my witness did give very broad answers and brought us in a very difficult position. He is now answering more clearly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, Mr. Simic, that -- I thought, Mr. Simic, that you were going to say that you would like two or three minutes more and that you would be ending. Unfortunately, we're now going to make the break, and then you'll have the opportunity of continuing after the half hour break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Mr. Simic, please continue with clear questions to the witness. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Oklopcic, in your statement, over a period of five or six days, you frequently mentioned the name of Mr. Kuruzovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was Mr. Kuruzovic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the witness.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kuruzovic was the former director of the elementary school called the 16th of May, and he was the commander of the concentration camp in Trnopolje. He used to be my teacher, and so on. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also in your statement, you said that during your stay in Omarska, he visited Omarska on several occasions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also in your statement, on page 22 of the B/C/S version, page 29 of the English version, second paragraph, towards the end, I shall quote you -- you can check of course exactly what you said, so it would speed things up a bit -- you stated then that "Mr. Zeljko Meakic and Mr. Kvocka, during Mr. Kuruzovic's visit, were quiet and deferential in relation to Mr. Kuruzovic." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that Mr. Kuruzovic was a teacher and a professor.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a secondary school teacher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he employed in the police?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said in your statement that you assumed that Mr. Meakic and Mr. Kvocka were the chief of security and his deputy.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain why there would be this subordinate attitude of chiefs towards a person who is not in the chain of command or in the hierarchy, or in the same occupation, if you assumed they were?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me explain. Slobodan Kuruzovic had the rank of major in the former Yugoslav People's Army. And from the beginning he participated in the war in Croatia --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please just answer my question. You have opened an interesting question. Was there ever a command structure between the army and the police?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army and the police cooperated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was clear.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Talking about Mr. Kuruzovic, after you left Omarska, did you meet him again?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Trnopolje concentration camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Kuruzovic make any decisions regarding your release?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he have to do?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had to sign a release paper. No one could leave the Trnopolje concentration camp without the signature of Slobodan Kuruzovic on a release document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Meakic sign such a release paper?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he could not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now try and clarify a few points that are not quite clear from your testimony, regarding specific events. During your interview, you described an incident in connection with the killing of Mr. Nasic. You said that it occurred around the 10th of July.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A week or ten days after my arrival.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also described the event.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But during your testimony last week, you stated that after the event, that same evening, the prisoners were addressed by Mr. Meakic.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next day and the morning, but they were present that same evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us clear that up, then. You're saying that both Mr. Meakic and Mr. Kvocka were present in the Omarska camp when this incident occurred, when Mr. Nasic was killed.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who addressed the prisoners the next day?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zeljko Meakic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Mr. Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he did but I'm not quite sure. I know that both of them were present that same evening, Mr. Meakic and Mr. Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said very explicitly, Mr. Oklopcic, confirming your assumption regarding the position held by Mr. Meakic and Mr. Kvocka as commanders of the guards and deputy commanders, that they worked in different shifts of 24 hours each, that they took turns. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let me just, however, say that last time you said that they addressed the prisoners that same evening, but we won't go into that. I should like to go back to the events of the 30th of May, the event that you have described. I'm paraphrasing, almost quoting what you said. You said that the previous bus stopped, and you showed us where, that you waited to disembark; that at one point shooting broke out; that you had to bend down your heads; that you didn't see anything, you just heard it; when you got off you saw blood being washed; you went to Mujo's room and you heard that in the shooting, a father and son, Avdo and Asaf Kapetanovic, had been killed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Oklopcic, on page 4 of your statement, second paragraph, in the English version, page 5, second paragraph, you explicitly stated: "I saw, when Cigo opened fire from an automatic weapon on a group of persons who were all five metres away from Cigo. They were waiting for their turn to stand up against the wall like the other persons in their group. I was 15 to 20 metres away. I saw that Avdo Kapetanovic and his son Asaf Kapetanovic were hit and fell immediately after the shooting. Panic was created in the group." Mr. Oklopcic, a moment ago you explained to Mr. Nikolic that this statement was the result of 50 or 60 hours of interviewing. Which of the two is true regarding the event of the 30th of May, 1992, what you told during your testimony or what you explicitly described in your statement? The position, where you stood, what you saw, and the men falling.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The real truth is what I described here in court. I didn't know Cigo, nor did I see Cigo kill anyone. I could have insisted on this statement. I'm sure it was a mistake. I often had different interpreters, they changed. The truth is I didn't see Cigo kill them, I didn't see the two -- the father and son die. It was only later on that I learnt about it from other people when I entered the room. That is the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I had to mention this because it is stated clearly in your statement, but let's move on. I should like to go back to the killings in July, and that will bring to an end my cross-examination. You stated that you were an eyewitness of the beating of Mr. Ramadanovic, nickname Cifut. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. No, "Cigut" is another name for a dish. So Mr. Krstic made a mistake and said "Cigut" instead of "Cifut".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You still claim that Mr. Ramadanovic died from the consequences of this beating.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. Not only that beating, but the one that preceded it as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Ramadanovic?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Extremely well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have any health problems?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was an elderly man. But whether he had any health problems, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After Mr. Ramadanovic, you also referred to an incident with Mr. Rizo Hadzalic, also in July.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.
