utterances.text: Did you inform the Tribunal of your change of opinion, as the first is different from this one? When did you change your attitude to this incident?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what it says there. I've just got a copy here. I know what I said on the occasion, and the truth is what I said when I was interviewed on the first day here, in this courtroom, when I was questioned in this courtroom on the first day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for interrupting, Mr. Stojanovic. But if you see any contradiction between the different statements of the witness and testimonies, you can ask a direct question to clarify the matter. Otherwise, you enter into argument with the witness. So ask him a direct question. "You said that then, this now. What do you say now at this point?" As we are all here now and it is an oral principle of oral testimony, so without going into a process of argumentation, ask direct questions. Otherwise, we'll never leave this courtroom, Mr. Stojanovic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I am doing my best to clear up the contradictions and have them explained in the simplest manner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next contradiction is the following. In all statements so far --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and let's see the results, because you're going to make the effort and we'll see the results, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In all statements given so far, Mr. Oklopcic, you make no mention of this particular incident with Emir Beganovic, but you did mention it for the first time in front of this Tribunal during your present testimony and examination.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't have time to say many things on the first day, that's how it was. So just as I did not mention Emir Beganovic up until that time, I didn't do many other things when I was questioned that day. So you must understand that it's not simple to come here, either for me or for you or for anybody else. And to make matters clearer, let me say that I know Rezak and Began very well, we were neighbours. So there is no doubt whatsoever that -- I'm not saying something that is contradictory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, now you have muddled me even further. I was a bit mixed up by your initial statements. Had you written down what you're saying now, there would be no misunderstanding. Very well. Having witnessed the incident, can you tell us what Zigic's appearance was like at the time? And when I say this, I mean the uniform he was wearing, or perhaps some characteristic personal traits, and so on.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, Zigic had a red cap. We said -- he called it a French cap in the former Yugoslavia, you know what it looks like, and he had an olive-green military uniform on him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have any bandages on any part of his body?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult for me to remember, for me to be able to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That means you can't remember. Very well. How did you recognise him? Did you know him from before?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and I've already answered that question. I said that I knew Zigic from before, but we were not personal friends or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't think we said specifically what time that was. You said in the course of the day that you were standing in a restaurant five, six, or eight hours, but what month was that, or part of a month?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the end of June, beginning of July. It's difficult for me to tell you exactly now after eight years have gone by. But it was in the late afternoon, which means between 6.00 and 8.00. How come I know this? I know this because at that time we would be made to go into the central building, where the canteen was situated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I'm right, you said before this Tribunal that, during this incident, Tadic was present as well, I mean Dusko Tadic.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know I said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did I hear that correctly? I do believe you said that.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think you heard correctly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, these people, and I'm thinking of Mr. Hukanovic, Kapetanovic, and others, did anybody ride on their backs during this incident?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I remember most vividly is what I describe. When Rezak was ordered, Hukanovic, to kneel down on the pista and to drink a puddle of dirty water which was on the pista at that time and to wash himself with that dirty water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you didn't notice anything else which would indicate any similar type of behaviour, inhumane anyway.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I did notice is that they were covered in blood, that they were dirty, that they had been beaten, and that they were exhausted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you knew Zigic because he worked in Croatia for a time and then came back to work as a taxi driver.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know him when he worked in Croatia, but I knew him when he worked as a taxi driver.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when this was?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was prior to the war, just before the war. And when we were in Trnopolje, when Zigic lined us up, he told us that publicly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. We'll get to Trnopolje in due course. If I'm not mistaken, you categorically said that you arrived in Trnopolje on the 5th of August and not the 3rd of August, as exists in some documents and we accept that. But you say that in the afternoon in Trnopolje, the representatives of the International Red Cross arrived and journalists from well-known newspaper houses in the world. Can you tell us how long they stayed? Did they stay a long time?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We arrived from Omarska at about 11.00 or 12.00, and at that time none of the International Red Cross representatives were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said it was in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were they there?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were there for two or three hours in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Two or three hours. Very well.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my opinion, as far as I'm able to recollect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the end of your statement, written statement, you say you were exchanged. Can you explain what this meant? Exchanged for whom, why you were exchanged?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can do that. You know that I had to fill in a form as soon as possible to leave, and after I left Trnopolje I had to leave Prijedor at the earliest opportunity. As I and my family were not able to leave in any other way --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise. I'm talking about the very act of exchange. Who were you exchanged for?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're not letting me explain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Perhaps it is too involved.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But this is an essential, vital question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went to Banja Luka, and at that time there was a woman called Perka [phoen], or something like that, in Banja Luka, and she transferred civilians towards Vlasic from Banja Luka. And on five buses, I and my family were in one of those buses, and we came to the plateau of Mount Vlasic. When we got there, there was a bus which had come from the direction of Travnik with only 10 or 15 people in that other bus. And this was supposed to be an exchange, five buses of us from the Serbian part and one bus coming from Travnik, or wherever. And as I say, in that other bus, there were only 10 or 15 people, not more than that, whereas our buses, our five buses were jam packed with people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These 10 to 15 people, what were they, civilians?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You have drawn up a list of the most responsible people, and my learned colleague, Mr. Jovan Simic, presented that list before me. It is a list compiled in handwriting. You gave that list to the Prosecution. Do you mention Zoran Zigic on that list?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. If it's there, then right; if not, then there's no problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on that list, did you mention expressly who killed Becir Medjunjanin? Do you make mention of that? But you stand by what you said there?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. It just says here that Becir Medjunjanin was killed in the month of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about the list. Look at page 2 of the list.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here it is, yes Becir Medjunjanin killed in July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does it say under that?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Killed by a man named Duca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you stand by that, do you?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us go back to another question, that is to say, one of your answers. You said you saw Zigic some ten times in Omarska. Do you remember any incident with respect to those ten times, except the one that we have just been talking about?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he there when Becir Medjunjanin was killed?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Zigic? No, I think he was not. I didn't see him close by.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when Hankin was killed?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also not. I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Stojanovic. Thank you very much. Mr. Keegan, do you have any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Proceed, then, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Re-examined by Mr. Keegan:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Oklopcic, in the cross-examination, in one of your answers you indicated that none of the regular policemen in the Omarska camp stood guard. What did the regular policemen do in the camp?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They brought in daily from Prijedor a couple of prisoners, five, six, four, it depended, and handed them over to these people who were in the Omarska concentration camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, speaking of the individuals who worked at the camp themselves who were regular policemen, you named among them Kvocka and Radic.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there others who were regular policemen before working in the camp that you know of?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would see regular policemen who would come into the camp and hand over these prisoners. Whether there were more of them, I don't know the answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to the questions with respect to Stupar, you mentioned that he spoke to a man named Rosic in the camp.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what position or duty Rosic had in the camp?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stupar told me that this Rosic had one of the main roles in Omarska, in the so-called Crisis Staff or something, but if he wanted to, he could help me. And he insisted and really tried to help me get out of the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This Rosic, did he work in the camp? Did he have a position in the camp itself that you know of?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I should say that there are two guys with the same surname. This Rosic, one was a guard, and this other one that Stupar spoke to, he came only two or three times to Omarska and he spoke to the investigators up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's this second Rosic that Mr. Stupar talked to.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to Slobodan Kuruzovic, were you aware if he was a member of the Crisis Staff in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of whether he had a position of authority or command in the Prijedor Territorial Defence after the takeover?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to the beating of Riza Hadzalic, is it possible that at the time he was outside on the pista, prior to the beating, that he himself had had something to eat with him or was eating something?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not have anything on him, nor was he eating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to Mr. Timarac, whom you mentioned came to the camp, and you said in response, in cross-examination, that he came to the camp to abuse prisoners. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any time did you see any of the camp personnel or authorities, command personnel in the camp, try to intervene with Mr. Timarac or to stop him in any way from abusing prisoners?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to the beating of Becir Medjunjanin, were you able to see who -- let me ask this: Is it possible that there were other persons with Duca and Timarac in the "white house" that you did not see because they were in the other rooms?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to the occasions on which you saw Zoran Zigic and Duca Knezevic in the Omarska camp, did you ever see any of the camp personnel or any of the command staff in the camp try and intervene or to stop them in any way from maltreating or assaulting prisoners?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw them, but no one tried to prevent it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to your 1994 statement, ICTY statement, that's been admitted into evidence, if we could clarify the procedures involved there. You have said that over the period of 22 through 26 September, that the investigators questioned you for approximately eight hours a day.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you discussed many things.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You signed this statement on the 10th of December, 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the procedure, as you have acknowledged at the end of that statement, indicates that this statement was read back to you by an interpreter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. Yes, Mr. Nikolic. What is the objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence was patient and did not react immediately, but we have a whole series of questions which were not unclear from the cross-examination. The witness has answered all these questions that Mr. Keegan is asking. He's just confirming what he has already answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Keegan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm addressing, in point of fact, the one part of the questions about the statement that were not asked, which is how did the witness certify the statement. They have tried to point to what they see as errors in the statement as to what the witness testified or things he said, but for some reason do not appear. I'm simply trying to bring the point that the interview was actually conducted over a week in September, and then several months later in December, the statement was read back to the witness and he signed it. I'm trying to clarify that that was, in fact, what occurred, and that it wasn't a situation where it was read back immediately to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Nikolic, you yourself put all these questions. I think Mr. Keegan is right to clarify these points. So Mr. Keegan, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Oklopcic, if I can recapture the last question. As indicated by the certification on your statement, was the statement, in fact, read back to you in a language you understood on the 12th of December, 1994?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I had that backwards. The 10th of December, not the 12th. Excuse.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: December. Yes. Yes, the 10th, I think it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness has already answered this question, Mr. Keegan. He has confirmed that he signed it on the 10th of December, 1994. Go on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm just trying to clarify this situation. The importance of the signature is when the statement was actually read back to him in a language that he understood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That it was read back to you on the 10th of December.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Keegan. We should like to truly finish the testimony of Mr. Oklopcic, and that is why I'm asking whether we can work a little longer, for ten minutes, so that the Judges can put their questions. I see a nod from the booths. So Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Oklopcic.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to have some clarifications from you to throw light on your testimony. First of all, some small questions regarding details. You said, I'll begin from the beginning, that when you left towards the hotel -- what was the name of the hotel?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hotel Balkan in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Hotel Balkan. You saw bodies in the street, and your son drew your attention to them. Were they bodies of military men or civilians?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Civilians. And then you heard the soldiers speaking the Ekavica dialect, and you said it was spoken in various places. How were they dressed? Were they military men? Because military men have different uniforms depending on the country they come from.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How were you able to judge their clothing? Which did they belong to?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Blue, green, camouflage, SMB olive-grey uniforms, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps you knew the different uniforms. Which army was this, did they belong to?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. The Yugoslav army. So if I understood you well, Mr. Kvocka was the deputy to the commander Meakic, and they changed every 24 hours. Was there a change in atmosphere in the camp or in the treatment of prisoners depending on who was on duty, Meakic or Kvocka? When did you feel better as human beings?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Mr. Kvocka was on duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then if I understood you well. Mr. Prcac replaced Mr. Kvocka later on. Did the situation improve under Mr. Prcac, or did it worsen?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, for me personally, the last 15 days or so of my stay in the camp, the Omarska concentration camp, was much better than at the beginning of my stay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those last 15 days were under whose command?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the command of Zeljko Meakic and Prcac. But I must clarify why for you to have a proper understanding. My group, a group of 70 men, was separated and their names read out on the 28th of July, and we were separated from all the other prisoners and put on the pista. At that time, while we were waiting, until the 5th of August, Mr. Ckalja approached me, the leader of one of the groups, and said, "Azedin, today or tomorrow an international organisation is due to come which will carry out an inspection here." They called me Uco, which is short for teacher, and they said, "Uco, do you understand what you have to do when talking to your friends?" I said, "I do." "And what will you say," Kvocka asked. I said that I was okay, that nobody is beating me, that we have enough food, and that nobody is mistreating us. And he answered, "I see that you are a clever guy and you will convey this to your colleagues." I went back and conveyed the message to my colleagues, and they all understood what needed to be said, except for one man who said, "No, I will not do that. I will tell the truth." I said, "Well, do that if you're ready to disappear, do as you will."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your objection now? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Mr. Oklopcic was talking about Mr. Ckalja, and he said Mr. Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's a slip of the tongue. I meant Ckalja, Ckalja. I'm sorry. I apologise. It wasn't Mr. Kvocka, it was Ckalja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Mr. Simic. So the correction will be made. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Oklopcic, try and give me coherent answers to my questions. You said that the treatment changed and that it was better under Kvocka's command than Meakic's, and you also said that that depended on each of the shifts. For instance, you mentioned that Krkan's team was the cruelest, and it was under his command that Riza Hukanovic was killed, and some others. Were these teams independent from the command, or was there a certain hierarchy of discipline? Did each team do what they wanted under their team leader, or did they have to answer to somebody above?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer this question with precision; however, my answer will be as follows: The guard shifts were never left to their own resources. There was always present the person who was in charge of that guard -- shift of guards. Whether they coordinated or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In other words, if, for instance, the leader was Meakic, of whom you said he was the worst, could the shift leader be tolerant or less severe in his treatment, or did he have to act in accordance with their chief, and vice versa? When Kvocka was on duty, did the shift leaders have a certain degree of freedom of action to do what they could? If you can answer it, that's fine. If not, just tell us you cannot.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the answer is both yes and no. I was never present at an incident involving Mr. Kvocka, beating or something else. I was never present when Mr. Radic was involved in beating. I was never present when Krle or Prcac were involved. But these things did happen during their shift. Who gave the orders, I really don't know and I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you could feel whether there was any discipline or not in the camp, or was it sort of an anarchy when each soldier could amuse himself as he wanted?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was discipline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was discipline. And within that framework, Krkan's team was the cruelest, as you said.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Concerning Mr. Kvocka, you indicated that he protected his brother-in-law Riza --

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His brother-in-law Riza, and he separated him from the others in public. Could any soldier protect somebody in a public manner like that, or only if he had a certain degree of authority? I don't know that, but Mr. Kvocka did that, and not only him, but two other brothers-in-law, my neighbours and friends. But at that time it was very difficult to release anyone from the prison; it was almost impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And he released them?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He took them away somewhere. They did not enter the room with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you see anyone else protecting somebody?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You often said that each shift had a certain attitude. How could you distinguish between the teams or shifts?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hardly at all. But it is a fact that the worst killings, which I saw and experienced, occurred when Krkan's shift was on duty. And another thing, if I may say in quotation marks, "I felt best when the shift from Maricka was on duty as I knew some of the parents of my former students and my former students." But this applies only to me personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But when you say "Krkan's shift," how did you know it was Krkan's shift?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I knew almost all the guards and which shift they were in. Every guard leader would take over duty at the same time as the guards and hand over duty 12 hours later to the next shift.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but the shift leader was not present during the tortures and the beatings.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you consider complaining to the shift leader?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had no chance to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question. The majority of prisoners, were they military men, soldiers, Muslim soldiers, or civilians, according to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Oklopcic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Fouad Riad. Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Oklopcic, you referred in your testimony many times to shifts, whether it's Krkan's shifts or Krle's shifts. Now, was it the common practice for all the people detained in the camp to refer to a shift by the name of the shift leader? In other words, if somebody said "Krkan's shift," did that mean Krkan was the shift leader?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. The next question is: You say on your paper that you drew up that the shifts changed every 12 hours, and I think you said that in your testimony as well. Since there were three shifts, does that mean that more than one shift was on duty at any one time, or were they over a period of a couple of days, so that you didn't have every shift on duty every 24-hour period? Was there more than one shift on duty at a single time?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but let me explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the shifts lasted from 7.00 a.m. to 7.00 p.m. and from 7.00 p.m. to 7.00 a.m., so in the course of one day, or 24 hours, two shifts would be on duty. The third shift would be resting for a day and then come to work the next day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. I understand. Thank you. The final question on that was: Did Krkan's shift typically come on in the daytime or the night-time, or did it sometimes day and sometimes night, Krkan's shift?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I wrote down, all the killings that I attended occurred in broad daylight. What happened in the evenings, perhaps somebody else will tell you about that who knows more about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: My question, though, was just: When Krkan's shift was on duty, was it usually the daytime? Is that what you're telling me? Just when Krkan's shift was on duty, was it usually in the day or at night?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, if Krkan's shift would start in the morning, or any other shift started in the morning, it would be from 7.00 until 7.00, and then the next day, that same shift would be coming from 7.00 in the evening until 7.00 in the morning. So there was a system of rotation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right. That's what I wanted to know. Now, you also testified that on one occasion in July, there was an official delegation from Republika Srpska that came to visit the camp, and when asked who was present from the camp leadership, you said -- at least it came through on the transcript -- "the commanders and deputy commanders." Now, did you mean by that more than one commander and more than one deputy commander, or was that a mistake, perhaps, in the translation? If so, who actually was there from the camp leadership in July when they came from Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Almost everyone who meant anything in the camp; the wardens and the shift leaders were present. I also said "others." From Prijedor, there was Major Slobodan Kuruzovic; from Prijedor also, Simo Miskovic. So I was implying all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right. But I'm most interested in the camp leadership that you remember being there on that occasion. Was Meakic there?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Who else was there from the camp leadership, besides the shift commanders and Meakic?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the camp leadership, Meakic and Kvocka were the leaders, the chief and the deputy, with the exception of the shift leaders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And that was in July; right?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you also testified that Brk appeared to be very close, the right-hand man of Meakic. How were you able to distinguish between a person like Kvocka or Prcac and Brk? What was different about Brk, who you say was so close to Meakic, that didn't make you think he was a deputy commander but did make you think that Kvocka and Prcac were deputy commanders?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first place, Brk, as they called him, would beat the prisoners, and he was always close to Zeljko Meakic. I said a moment ago that I never saw Kvocka or Prcac beat anyone, as far as I am aware. But Brk, I think his surname is Tadic, known as Brk, he would enter and beat the prisoners. On one occasion, when Becir Medjunjanin and his wife and child were brought in, both he and Zeljko Meakic beat them. So he always moved around with Zeljko Meakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. So he was more, according to your impressions, like a staff person, an aid to Meakic, than a person with his own command down the line, such as a deputy commander would have?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. Last question. You mentioned that Medjunjanin's wife and child were beaten on their arrival at Omarska. How old was the child, approximately? And that is your testimony, that the child was actually beaten?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A young man. A young man, 18 or 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. How old was Hankin? You referred to him as a young man, but is he about the same age, younger?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was older. I was 31 or 32 at the time, and he was two or three years my senior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Wald. I am perhaps at an advantage to be the last to put questions as most of the questions have already been asked. Nevertheless, I have two or three minor questions. You answered my colleague Judge Fouad Riad that you managed to identify the guards belonging to the Krkan shift because you knew them. How did you identify the guards in the other shifts?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I didn't know them in person before I arrived at the Omarska concentration camp. And how I came to know them was because they called each other by name in public, Zoka, Paspalj, Kricka, Savic, and so on. A second shift, another shift, the shifts from Maricka, as I explained earlier on, was the shift in which there were six to eight of my students and two or three parents of former students. And the third shift, a shift from Omarska, there were a couple of football players that I played against when we had matches between Prijedor and Omarska. So it wasn't difficult for me to identify them at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My second question is the following: At a given point in time, you mentioned Mujo's building or Mujo's room, and they said that there were two Mujos. Why did they choose the name Mujo?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because in that shift -- no, I mean in that room that was referred to as Mujo's room, there were all prisoners who came from the centre of town, Stari Grad, Raskovac, Skela, those districts in town. And Mujo was the so-called representative of that room, that large room, and he took those people out to lunch. He would line them up, 30 by 30, and so on. Later on he was joined by Burho. Now, why it wasn't called Burho's room, I don't know. It doesn't matter. It was called Mujo's room. And one night, on the 28th of July, when the two of them disappeared, I took over this shift -- not shift, I mean this group of prisoners, taking them to lunch, I was at the head of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The food of the guards was different from the food you got. How do you know that? How do you know that their food was different?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I described what we ate; that is to say, that we would get a piece of bread and had a soup of some kind, made out of a little bit of potato, a little bit of cabbage, and the third time there were beans. The guards would get a different type of food. They would get schnitzels, meat, because the cattle would be slaughtered. Cows were brought from Kozarac, and the prisoners who were butchers by profession or knew something about the butcher's trade went to sort out all this meat that came in. Thirdly, when we had our snacks at around 11.00 or 12.00, they would be brought different snacks with coffee, beer, cigarettes, a form of sandwich with salami or cheese or whatever. So that's a big difference between the food they ate and the food we were given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Oklopcic, you mentioned at one point that the guards were drunk. I must say that I have difficulty in formulating this question, but in your opinion, drunkenness, a state of intoxication, was it by chance or was it regular practice, encouraged? Or is there another hypothesis?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can just say one thing, and that is that the guards were far more aggressive when they were drunk. Whether that was encouraged or not, I think it was, but you can understand me when I say that I can't answer that question. But they were far more aggressive when they drank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So to restate my question, it is true, from your point of view, that when the guards were under the effects, they were more aggressive.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness Oklopcic, you have answered many questions asked of you by the Prosecution, by the Defence, by the Judges; you have spent a long time here in The Hague. Have you got something to say which has not yet been asked of you and you'd like to say it? Briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to say something about a question asked of me by Mr. Fila, and I assumed that one of the attorneys would ask me that; not only from the side of the Defence, but also from the side of the Prosecution, and perhaps the Judges as well. I truly did try, Your Honours, to present the truth, and what I have stated here was the truth. When Mr. Fila asked me whether I hate, then I say I hate, and I must hate. But let me repeat once again: The gentlemen sitting here and the others who sat here never in my life would do to them what they did to me and my people and others. And I hope that they will get the sentence they deserve, given to them by God and by you yourselves and by everyone else. And I thank you, one and all; I thank my own attorneys, the gentlemen who defended them. I think that we have cooperated in a proper and correct manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Very well. We've put that correction as to the name mentioned. The Tribunal is here to analyse and to judge actions committed by individuals, and we should like to note that you were not capable of doing the same thing. Things did happen, but what we must ensure is that none of that is ever repeated, to you or anybody else. Thank you, Mr. Oklopcic, for coming here, thank you for your cooperation, and we apologise for having had to inconvenience you in bringing you here. But thank you again. We are going to adjourn the hearing and continue tomorrow morning at 9.30. Are you ready, Madam Hollis, for tomorrow morning, 9.30?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we are. Perhaps when the witness excuses himself, Mr. Keegan can raise to you orally a matter that involves a witness who will be called later. It's an oral motion, and we have conferred with the Defence

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Keegan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I realise we've already gone over time. We would just like to raise that we do have a motion for protective measures for an upcoming witness, and I leave it to Your Honours whether you'd like to take it up this afternoon or perhaps first thing in the morning. We would like to do it orally and get a decision because it will affect the witness who will be called at the end of this week. So obviously the outcome -- your decision on the motion will affect whether the witness is called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon. Let me try and understand. You're telling us that you're going to present the witness if we accord the protective measures, or we're going to have the witness tomorrow and then we're going to discuss protective measures? What were you saying actually?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Right now the witness is scheduled to be called at the end of this week. We need to present the motion now so that we will be able to advise the witness of the outcome of your decision on the motion prior to them travelling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I think that we need to go into private session, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let us move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: 3.05 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 16th day of May, 2000, at 9.30 a.m. 25
